feed.title: Concepts
feed.subtitle: Engineering ideas you understand by changing the inputs.

entry.title: Calibration
entry.summary: A model is calibrated when the things it calls 90% likely happen about 90% of the time, which you check by grouping its decisions by stated confidence and counting how often each group is right.

entry.title: Decision models (System One)
entry.summary: A decision model does not write text: it reads a situation and returns one probability for each option on a list you give it, in a single pass, so code can act on the answer.

entry.title: Encoder, decoder, or both
entry.summary: Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder transformers are the same attention with different masks that decide which tokens each token may look at, and that choice decides whether the model can write text.

entry.title: Spaced repetition
entry.summary: Spaced repetition reviews a fact just as you are about to forget it, which strengthens the memory more than reviewing it often, so the gaps between reviews can grow and the total effort stays small.

entry.title: Quantization
entry.summary: Quantization stores each weight in fewer bits by rounding it to the nearest of a few levels, trading a small error for a model that is several times smaller.

entry.title: Tokenization
entry.summary: A tokenizer cuts text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary learned from data, so text it saw often becomes few tokens and text it rarely saw becomes many, which is why the same sentence costs more in some languages.

entry.title: KV cache
entry.summary: A language model saves the keys and values of tokens it has already read, so each new token costs one pass instead of a rerun of everything before it, and pays for that in memory that grows with every token.

entry.title: LoRA
entry.summary: LoRA fine-tunes a large model by freezing its weights and learning a small low-rank update, a product of two thin matrices, so far fewer numbers are trained.

entry.title: RLHF
entry.summary: RLHF tunes a language model toward what people prefer by training a reward model on human comparisons, then pushing the model toward high reward while a KL penalty keeps it near where it started.

entry.title: Reinforcement learning
entry.summary: An agent learns what to do by trying actions and seeing rewards, with credit for a late reward flowing back to the earlier steps that led to it.

entry.title: Attention
entry.summary: Attention lets each word in a sequence take a weighted mix of the other words, with the weights set by how well they match what it is looking for.

entry.title: Contamination and Goodhart
entry.summary: When benchmark questions leak into a model’s training data, the benchmark score overstates what the model can do; a fresh test of the same kind shows the gap.

entry.title: Online evals and A/B tests
entry.summary: An online eval compares two versions on live traffic; how many users it needs depends on the lift you want to see, and checking the result early inflates false wins.

entry.title: Agent evals
entry.summary: An agent is graded on what it did, not just what it said: success is checked on the final state, reliability is checked by running each task many times and requiring all runs to work.

entry.title: RAG evals
entry.summary: A RAG answer can fail in the retrieval step, in the generation step, or in both, so a RAG eval grades the retrieved context, the answer’s faithfulness to it, and the answer’s relevance separately.

entry.title: Human agreement and kappa
entry.summary: Cohen’s kappa measures how much two raters agree beyond what luck would give; raw percent agreement can look high when the labels are lopsided.

entry.title: Pairwise preference and Elo
entry.summary: Ranking by head-to-head votes: each vote moves two ratings, Elo does it one vote at a time, and a Bradley-Terry fit uses all votes at once.

entry.title: LLM as judge
entry.summary: An LLM judge grades another model’s answers cheaply and agrees with experts about as often as experts agree with each other, but it has measurable biases: it favours the answer shown first and the longer answer.

entry.title: pass@k
entry.summary: pass@k is the chance that at least one of k generated programs passes the tests; it is estimated from n samples by counting the ways to draw k without replacement.

entry.title: Precision, recall and reciprocal rank
entry.summary: Precision@k, recall@k and reciprocal rank grade the same ranked list in three ways: how clean the top k is, how much of the good material it found, and how early the first good result appears.

entry.title: Exact match and F1
entry.summary: Exact match checks whether an answer equals the reference after cleaning; F1 gives partial credit for the words they share.

entry.title: Is 82% better than 80%?
entry.summary: An eval score is a guess from a sample of questions, so it has error bars; two models are only different when the range of their gap stays away from zero.

entry.title: The map of evals
entry.summary: Every eval answers what is being graded, who or what grades it, and when; this map shows where each eval page fits and what each one cannot see.

entry.title: nDCG@k
entry.summary: nDCG@k scores a ranked list: each result earns its grade, shrunk by its rank, divided by the best score the same results could earn.

entry.title: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder
entry.summary: A bi-encoder reads the query and each document separately, so document vectors can be saved ahead of time; a cross-encoder reads them together, so it must run once per document, per search.

entry.title: BM25 and the inverted index
entry.summary: BM25 ranks documents for a search: rare words count more, repeats count a little, and long documents lose points. An index finds the right documents fast.
